criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains the real mechanisms - producer/consumer decoupling, buffering/load-leveling of spikes, independent worker scaling, and durable retry/back-pressure - and correctly characterises at-least-once delivery and the resulting idempotency requirement. No factual errors such as claiming the queue lowers a single request's end-to-end latency or that the queue guarantees exactly-once delivery.

Covers both halves of the prompt: several distinct benefits of the queue AND at least one concrete consequence/risk paired with a mitigation. Full marks also acknowledge the asynchronous-result implication (client must poll/be notified) or dead-letter-queue / monitoring handling.
Explains WHY each property follows - why buffering prevents connection exhaustion and turns bursts into queue depth, why at-least-once delivery forces idempotency - rather than just listing keywords.

A teammate could act on the explanation: organised, uses terminology (visibility timeout, dead-letter queue, idempotency, back-pressure) correctly and in context, and clearly separates the benefits from the risk-and-mitigation.

expected_answer_points: The queue decouples the API from the slow workers so the API can accept the request and respond immediately (e.g. 202 with a job id) instead of holding a connection open for the whole 30-90s LLM call, which stops connection/thread-pool exhaustion.
The queue buffers / load-levels spikes: a burst becomes accumulated queue depth that workers drain at a steady sustainable rate, rather than overwhelming the worker or API tier all at once.
Workers can be scaled independently of the API (e.g. add consumers or auto-scale on queue depth) to work down a backlog.
Messages are held durably, giving back-pressure and resilience: if workers are slow or down, jobs wait in the queue and can be retried instead of being dropped.

Names a real consequence: delivery is typically at-least-once, so a job can be redelivered (e.g. after a crash or visibility-timeout expiry) and processed more than once, which requires idempotent consumers / deduplication on a job id.

Addresses further failure handling and the async trade-off: a dead-letter queue for repeatedly failing 'poison' messages, monitoring of queue depth / oldest-message age, and that the client now gets its result asynchronously (must poll or be notified).
common_pitfalls: Says only 'it makes the API faster / asynchronous' without explaining the underlying mechanism (decoupling, buffering, independent scaling), giving a vague non-answer.

Claims the queue reduces the latency of an individual job - it does not; end-to-end time per request is unchanged or slightly higher, and the win is throughput, stability, and availability under load.

Assumes exactly-once delivery and never mentions idempotency or deduplication, so duplicate processing (double writes / double charges from redelivery after a visibility-timeout expiry or crash) goes unaddressed.
Confuses the message queue with a load balancer, treating it as something that distributes synchronous requests across workers rather than buffering asynchronous work.
Forgets that the client no longer gets a synchronous result and must poll or be notified for the outcome.
Overlooks poison messages / the need for a dead-letter queue and queue-depth monitoring, so a permanently failing job silently retries forever or stalls the backlog.
reference_answer:
Putting a queue between the API and the workers turns a synchronous, blocking call into an asynchronous pipeline, and that helps in several ways.

Decoupling: the API's job becomes validate-and-enqueue. It returns immediately (typically 202 Accepted with a job id) instead of holding an HTTP connection open for the whole 30-90s LLM call, so it stops exhausting its connection/thread pool under load.

Load leveling: the queue is a buffer. A spike of requests accumulates as queued messages and workers drain them at their own sustainable rate, rather than the burst hitting the workers all at once. Traffic bursts become queue depth instead of timeouts.

Independent scaling and resilience: workers scale separately from the API - you can auto-scale consumers on queue depth to burn down a backlog, and if all workers are down the jobs sit durably in the queue and get retried instead of being lost. That gives back-pressure.

Main consequence: managed queues like SQS (standard) deliver at-least-once. A message can be redelivered - e.g. if a worker crashes or exceeds the visibility timeout before deleting it - so the same job may be processed more than once. Consumers must therefore be idempotent (dedupe on the job/idempotency id) so duplicates don't double-charge or write twice. I'd also add a dead-letter queue for messages that keep failing, alarm on queue depth / age of the oldest message, and give clients a way to poll or be notified, since the result is now asynchronous.
